questions.text: All poets are dreamers. All dreamers are optimists. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
questions.explanation: Two universal affirmative premises linked by the middle term 'dreamers' yield the universal conclusion that every poet is an optimist.

questions.text: No reptiles are mammals. All cobras are reptiles. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
questions.explanation: Cobras fall entirely within the class of reptiles, and that class is wholly excluded from mammals, so no cobra can be a mammal.

questions.text: Some students are athletes. All athletes are disciplined. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
questions.explanation: The students who are athletes must share every property of athletes, so at least some students are disciplined; nothing is proved about the rest.

questions.text: All squares are rectangles. Some rectangles are red. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
questions.explanation: A particular affirmative statement can be converted, so 'some rectangles are red' gives 'some red things are rectangles'; the premises never link squares to colour.

questions.text: All doctors are graduates. No graduate is illiterate. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
questions.explanation: Doctors are contained in the class of graduates, and that class is entirely excluded from the illiterate, so no doctor is illiterate.

questions.text: From the statement 'Some books are novels', which conclusion necessarily follows?
questions.explanation: A particular affirmative proposition converts simply: if some books are novels then some novels are books.

questions.text: From the statement 'No politician is honest', which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: No honest person is a politician
questions.explanation: A universal negative proposition converts simply, so exclusion between the two classes holds in both directions.

questions.text: Given 'All mangoes are fruits', which statement does NOT follow?
options: Whatever is not a fruit is not a mango
questions.explanation: Reversing a universal affirmative is invalid; the other three are restatements or the contrapositive of the original.

questions.text: All A are B. All B are C. All C are D. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
questions.explanation: Class inclusion is transitive, so A is contained in B, B in C and C in D, placing every A inside D.

questions.text: No red object is cheap. Some pens are red. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
questions.explanation: The pens that are red belong to a class wholly excluded from cheap things, so at least those pens are not cheap.

questions.text: All metals conduct electricity. Copper is a metal. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
questions.explanation: An individual belonging to a class inherits every property asserted of the whole class.

questions.text: Only members may enter the club. Bilal entered the club. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
questions.explanation: 'Only members may enter' makes membership a necessary condition of entry, so anyone who entered must be a member.

questions.text: Everyone who passes the test receives a certificate. Ahmed did not receive a certificate. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: Ahmed did not sit the test
Ahmed did not pass the test
questions.explanation: This is modus tollens: denying the consequent of a conditional lets us deny its antecedent.

questions.text: In a categorical syllogism, the term that appears in both premises but not in the conclusion is called the
questions.explanation: The middle term links the two premises and is dropped from the conclusion; the major and minor terms are the predicate and subject of the conclusion.

questions.text: The argument 'All dogs are animals; all cats are animals; therefore all dogs are cats' commits the fallacy of
questions.explanation: The middle term 'animals' is not distributed in either premise, so the two classes are never actually connected.

questions.text: An argument is valid when
options: the conclusion must be true if the premises are true
its conclusion happens to be true
its premises happen to be true
questions.explanation: Validity is about the form of the inference: true premises cannot lead to a false conclusion in a valid argument.

questions.text: A sound argument is one that
options: is valid and has all true premises
has a true conclusion but false premises
questions.explanation: Soundness adds factual truth of the premises to formal validity.

questions.text: All soldiers are brave. Some brave persons are poets. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
questions.explanation: Only the second premise can be converted; nothing connects soldiers with poets because the middle term is undistributed.

questions.text: No teacher is lazy. All lazy persons are unpunctual. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: No lazy person is a teacher
questions.explanation: The first premise converts simply; the premises do not exclude teachers from the wider class of unpunctual persons.

questions.text: All P are Q. No Q are R. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
questions.explanation: Everything in P lies inside Q, and Q is wholly excluded from R, so P and R cannot overlap.

questions.text: Some officers are engineers. All engineers are graduates. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
questions.explanation: The officers who are engineers must also be graduates, which establishes a particular, not a universal, conclusion.

questions.text: The proverb 'All that glitters is not gold' is logically intended to mean
options: Some things that glitter are not gold
questions.explanation: The intended sense is the denial of a universal claim, which is a particular negative: not everything glittering is gold.

questions.text: Which statement is logically equivalent to 'If it rains, the match is cancelled'?
options: If it does not rain, the match is not cancelled
The match is cancelled only if it rains
If the match is not cancelled, it did not rain
If the match is cancelled, it rained
questions.explanation: A conditional is equivalent only to its contrapositive, formed by negating and interchanging antecedent and consequent.

questions.text: The contrapositive of 'If a number is divisible by 4, then it is even' is
options: If a number is even, then it is divisible by 4
If a number is not divisible by 4, then it is not even
If a number is odd, then it is divisible by 4
If a number is not even, then it is not divisible by 4
questions.explanation: The contrapositive negates both parts and reverses their order, and it always has the same truth value as the original.

questions.text: The converse of 'If x is a bird, then x has feathers' is
options: If x has feathers, then x is a bird
If x is not a bird, then x has no feathers
If x has no feathers, then x is not a bird
x is a bird and x has feathers
questions.explanation: The converse simply interchanges antecedent and consequent, and it does not follow from the original statement.

questions.text: If a metal is heated it expands. This metal did not expand. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: The metal is not really a metal
questions.explanation: Denying the consequent of a true conditional validly denies its antecedent (modus tollens).

questions.text: 'If a student cheats he is disqualified. Aslam was disqualified, therefore Aslam cheated.' This reasoning commits the fallacy of
questions.explanation: Disqualification may have other causes; inferring the antecedent from the consequent is invalid.

questions.text: 'If it snows the road is closed. It did not snow, therefore the road is not closed.' This reasoning commits the fallacy of
questions.explanation: The conditional says nothing about what happens when it does not snow, so the road may still be closed for another reason.

questions.text: Either the fuse is blown or the bulb is dead. The fuse is not blown. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: The bulb is in working order
questions.explanation: In a disjunctive syllogism, denying one alternative of a true disjunction establishes the other.

questions.text: If P then Q, and if Q then R. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: If not P then not R
questions.explanation: Conditionals chain together in a hypothetical syllogism, giving the transitive conditional from P to R.

questions.text: 'Only if you submit the form will you be registered.' This statement means that submitting the form is
questions.explanation: 'Only if' introduces a necessary condition; it does not promise that submission alone guarantees registration.

questions.text: Passing the written test is a necessary but not sufficient condition for appointment. It follows that
options: nobody who fails the test is appointed
everyone who passes the test is appointed
only those who fail the test are appointed
the test has no bearing on appointment
questions.explanation: A necessary condition must be met by every appointee, but meeting it does not by itself secure appointment.

questions.text: The correct denial of the statement 'All students passed' is
options: At least one student did not pass
questions.explanation: The contradictory of a universal affirmative is a particular negative, requiring only one exception.

questions.text: The correct denial of the statement 'Some birds can swim' is
questions.explanation: The contradictory of a particular affirmative is the universal negative covering every member of the class.

questions.text: The expression 'if and only if' states
options: both a necessary and a sufficient condition
questions.explanation: A biconditional asserts that each side implies the other, so the condition is both necessary and sufficient.

questions.text: 'No pass, no entry' is logically equivalent to
options: A pass may be shown after entry
If a person enters, that person has a pass
If a person has a pass, that person enters
questions.explanation: 'If no pass then no entry' is a conditional whose contrapositive is 'if entry then a pass'.

questions.text: A conditional statement and its contrapositive are
options: equivalent only when both are false
questions.explanation: Negating and interchanging the two parts preserves truth value in every case.

questions.text: Either the report is wrong or the machine is faulty. The machine is not faulty. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: The machine must still be replaced
Both the report and the machine are in order
questions.explanation: Eliminating one disjunct of a true disjunction leaves the other one standing.

questions.text: A is taller than B. C is shorter than B. Who is the tallest of the three?
options: B and C are of equal height
questions.explanation: A stands above B and B stands above C, so A occupies the top of the order.

questions.text: P is heavier than Q, Q is heavier than R, and R is heavier than S. Who is the lightest?
questions.explanation: The chain of comparisons runs P, Q, R, S from heaviest to lightest.

questions.text: X is older than Y and Y is older than Z. Which statement must be true?
questions.explanation: The 'older than' relation is transitive, so the order runs X, Y, Z from oldest to youngest.

questions.text: In a race Ali finished ahead of Bilal, Bilal finished ahead of Danish, and Danish finished ahead of Ehsan. Who finished last?
questions.explanation: The stated order is Ali, Bilal, Danish, Ehsan, so Ehsan is at the end of it.

questions.text: Amina scored more than Bushra, and Chanda scored less than Bushra. Which statement must be true?
options: Bushra scored the highest of the three
questions.explanation: Amina is above Bushra and Bushra is above Chanda, so Amina must be above Chanda.

questions.text: All members of the committee are lawyers. Sana is not a lawyer. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: Sana is not a member of the committee
Sana is a member of the committee
Some lawyers are not committee members
questions.explanation: Anyone outside the class of lawyers must lie outside the committee, which is contained in that class.

questions.text: Every book on the shelf is in Urdu. This dictionary is in English. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: This dictionary is not on the shelf
This dictionary is on the shelf
questions.explanation: An item lacking the property common to everything on the shelf cannot be on the shelf.

questions.text: No student in the class is above 20 years of age. Kamran is 22 years old. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: Kamran is not a student anywhere
Some students in the class are 22
Kamran is not in the class
questions.explanation: Kamran fails the age condition satisfied by every member of the class, so he cannot be a member.

questions.text: All the pens in the box are blue. This pen is red. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: This pen did not come from the box
This pen came from the box
The box contains some red pens
questions.explanation: Since every pen in the box is blue, a red pen must have some other source.

questions.text: Aslam is sitting between Bashir and Chand, and Bashir is to Aslam's left. Which statement must be true?
options: Aslam is at one end of the row
questions.explanation: Aslam has one neighbour on each side; with Bashir on the left, Chand must be on the right.

questions.text: Five persons stand in a row. Q is exactly in the middle and P stands immediately to Q's left. How many persons stand to the left of P?
questions.explanation: Q occupies the third place and P the second, so exactly one person stands to P's left.

questions.text: Whenever it rains the road becomes wet. The road is dry today. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: Rain does not affect the road
questions.explanation: If rain always produced a wet road, a dry road rules out rain (modus tollens).

questions.text: All A are B. No B is C. Some C are D. Which conclusion must be true?
questions.explanation: A lies wholly inside B and B is wholly outside C, so A and C cannot overlap; nothing follows about D.

questions.text: A man says, 'All my sons are engineers.' Rashid is his son. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
questions.explanation: A property asserted of every member of a group applies to any named member of it.

questions.text: 'Do not accept his economic plan; he failed in his own business years ago.' This argument commits the fallacy of
questions.explanation: The reasoning attacks the person's record instead of examining the merits of the plan itself.

questions.text: 'My opponent wants to reduce the defence budget, so clearly he wants the country left defenceless.' This is the fallacy of
questions.explanation: The opponent's position is exaggerated into an absurd version that is easier to attack.

questions.text: 'Nobody has ever proved that ghosts do not exist, so ghosts must exist.' This is the fallacy of
questions.explanation: Absence of disproof is treated as proof, which the argumentum ad ignorantiam wrongly allows.

questions.text: 'Millions of people buy this brand, so it must be the best.' This is the fallacy of
questions.explanation: Widespread acceptance is not evidence of quality; the argumentum ad populum substitutes numbers for reasons.

questions.text: 'Please raise my grade, sir; my family will be heartbroken if I fail.' This is the fallacy of
questions.explanation: Sympathy is offered in place of any evidence that the grade was wrongly awarded.

questions.text: 'Approve my proposal, or remember that your contract comes up for renewal next month.' This is the fallacy of
questions.explanation: A veiled threat, not evidence, is used to secure agreement (argumentum ad baculum).

questions.text: 'Either we abolish every subsidy or the economy will collapse.' This is the fallacy of
questions.explanation: Only two extreme options are presented although many intermediate possibilities exist.

questions.text: 'If students are allowed to retake one paper, they will soon demand to retake every paper and the examination system will collapse.' This is the fallacy of
questions.explanation: A chain of increasingly serious consequences is asserted without any evidence that the first step leads to the last.

questions.text: 'This law is just because it is right, and it is right because it is just.' This is the fallacy of
questions.explanation: The conclusion is used as its own support, so the argument moves in a closed circle.

questions.text: 'I wore my lucky shirt and the team won, so the shirt brought the victory.' This is the fallacy of
questions.explanation: Mere sequence in time is mistaken for a causal connection.

questions.text: 'I met two rude people from that city, so everyone there is rude.' This is the fallacy of
questions.explanation: A sweeping conclusion is drawn from a sample far too small to support it.

questions.text: 'Every player in the side is outstanding, so the side as a whole must be outstanding.' This is the fallacy of
questions.explanation: Properties of the individual parts are transferred without warrant to the whole.

questions.text: 'That is a very wealthy company, so every one of its employees must be wealthy.' This is the fallacy of
questions.explanation: A property of the whole is wrongly assigned to each of its parts.

questions.text: 'A feather is light; what is light cannot be dark; therefore a feather cannot be dark.' This is the fallacy of
questions.explanation: The word 'light' shifts from meaning low in weight to meaning pale in colour within the same argument.

questions.text: Asked about rising inflation, a speaker replies with a long description of the beauty of the northern areas. This is the fallacy of
questions.explanation: An irrelevant subject is introduced to draw attention away from the question asked.

questions.text: 'You advise me to give up smoking, but you smoke yourself, so your advice is worthless.' This is the fallacy of
questions.explanation: The adviser's own conduct is irrelevant to whether the advice is correct; this is the 'you too' form of ad hominem.

questions.text: 'A famous cricketer says this syrup cures diabetes, so it must cure diabetes.' This is the fallacy of
questions.explanation: The person cited is respected in a field unrelated to medicine, so his endorsement is not evidence.

questions.text: 'Running a country is exactly like running a household, so a government should never borrow money.' This is the fallacy of
questions.explanation: The two cases differ in essential respects, so the comparison cannot carry the conclusion.

questions.text: 'This practice must be wrong because it began during the colonial period.' This is the fallacy of
questions.explanation: The argument judges an idea by its origin rather than by its present merits.

questions.text: The fallacy of assuming that what is true of a whole must be true of each of its parts is called
questions.explanation: Division moves from whole to parts; composition moves in the opposite direction, from parts to whole.

questions.text: The fallacy of using the same word in two different senses within one argument is called
questions.explanation: Equivocation trades on an ambiguity of a single term; amphiboly arises from ambiguous grammar instead.

questions.text: The fallacy in which the conclusion is already assumed in the premises is known as
questions.explanation: Petitio principii offers as support the very claim that is supposed to be proved.

questions.text: The Latin phrase 'post hoc ergo propter hoc' means
options: after this, therefore because of this
questions.explanation: It names the error of treating a later event as caused by an earlier one merely because it followed.

questions.text: 'Argumentum ad hominem' literally means an argument directed
questions.explanation: The attack is aimed at the person advancing the claim rather than at the claim itself.

questions.text: 'Argumentum ad populum' is an appeal to
options: the beliefs or feelings of the crowd
questions.explanation: It urges acceptance of a claim because many people already accept it.

questions.text: 'Argumentum ad baculum' is an appeal to
questions.explanation: 'Baculum' means a stick, so the phrase names the appeal to coercion rather than to evidence.

questions.text: Statement: 'Take our tablet and your headache will disappear within ten minutes.' Which assumption is implicit in this statement?
options: People want quick relief from headache
Every tablet acts within ten minutes
Headache cannot be relieved in any other way
Our tablet is the cheapest available
questions.explanation: The appeal only works if speed of relief is something the reader values; the other statements go far beyond what is taken for granted.

questions.text: Statement: 'Boil the water before drinking it.' Which assumption is implicit in this statement?
options: Boiling improves the taste of water
All diseases are spread through water
Unboiled water may be unsafe to drink
questions.explanation: The advice makes sense only if the water as supplied carries some risk that boiling removes.

questions.text: Statement: 'The examination centre has been shifted to the college because more candidates applied this year.' Which assumption is implicit in this statement?
options: The old centre has been demolished
Candidates prefer colleges to other buildings
Examinations must always be held in colleges
The college can seat more candidates than the old centre
questions.explanation: The stated reason works only if the new venue solves the problem of extra candidates, that is, it has greater capacity.

questions.text: Statement: 'Submit the form before 5 p.m.; forms received later will not be accepted.' Which assumption is implicit in this statement?
options: Applicants are able to submit the form before 5 p.m.
No applicant will submit the form at all
The office remains closed during the day
questions.explanation: Setting a deadline presupposes that those addressed are in a position to meet it.

questions.text: Statement: 'In case of fire use the stairs; do not use the lift.' Which assumption is implicit in this statement?
options: Stairs are always wider than lifts
Fires break out only in tall buildings
Lifts are more expensive to run
The lift may become unsafe during a fire
questions.explanation: The instruction rests on the belief that the lift carries a risk in a fire that the stairs do not.

questions.text: Statement: 'Write your roll number on the answer sheet.' Which assumption is implicit in this statement?
options: Every candidate has been given a roll number
questions.explanation: The instruction can be obeyed only if each candidate actually possesses a roll number.

questions.text: Statement: 'The company has announced a bonus for workers in order to raise production.' Which assumption is implicit in this statement?
options: Production cannot be raised by any other means
questions.explanation: The measure presupposes a link between extra pay and extra output; the other options are not needed for the plan to make sense.

questions.text: Statement: 'Read the instructions on the packet before using this medicine.' Which assumption is implicit in this statement?
options: The medicine is dangerous in every dose
All users are trained in medicine
The instructions are printed in Urdu
questions.explanation: The direction assumes the existence of instructions on the packet; nothing else is required for it to be sensible.

questions.text: Statement: 'Because of the fuel shortage the government has advised offices to work four days a week.' Which assumption is implicit in this statement?
options: The shortage will last for ever
Working fewer days will reduce fuel consumption
questions.explanation: The advice is a means to an end and presupposes that the shorter week actually saves fuel.

questions.text: Statement: 'Buy a helmet and ride safely.' Which assumption is implicit in this statement?
options: Wearing a helmet makes riding safer
Riding without a helmet is impossible
questions.explanation: The advertisement links the purchase to safety, which presupposes that the helmet contributes to it.

questions.text: In the analysis of an argument, an assumption is
options: a definition of the terms used
something taken for granted but not stated
questions.explanation: An assumption is an unstated premise that the argument needs in order to work.

questions.text: Statement: 'Notice: all employees must attend the training session on Monday.' Which assumption is implicit in this statement?
options: Employees will be available on Monday
Employees know nothing about their work
questions.explanation: A compulsory session presupposes that those required to attend can in fact be present that day.

questions.text: Event A: the price of petrol was raised on Monday. Event B: taxi fares were increased on Tuesday. Which relation is most reasonable?
options: A is the cause and B is the effect
B is the cause and A is the effect
The two events are entirely unconnected
Both are effects of a fall in demand
questions.explanation: Fuel is a direct input cost for taxis, and the increase in fares followed the rise in price.

questions.text: Ice-cream sales and cases of heat stroke both rise sharply in June. The best explanation is that
options: heat stroke causes people to buy ice-cream
the two figures are recorded wrongly
both are effects of the hot weather
questions.explanation: A third factor, high temperature, produces both trends, so the correlation between them is not causal.

questions.text: The reasoning 'cities with more police also record more crime, therefore police cause crime' overlooks the principle that
options: correlation does not by itself establish causation
questions.explanation: Two things may vary together because one drives the other in the reverse direction or because a third factor drives both.

questions.text: A survey shows that students who sleep longer obtain higher marks. Which finding would most weaken the claim that extra sleep causes higher marks?
options: Sleep is necessary for good health
Well-organised students both sleep longer and study more effectively
questions.explanation: It supplies a common third factor that could produce both the longer sleep and the better marks.

questions.text: In a controlled experiment the purpose of the control group is
options: to reduce the cost of the experiment
to confirm what the researcher expects
to provide a comparison in which the suspected cause is absent
to increase the total number of participants
questions.explanation: Only by comparing with a group not exposed to the factor can a change be attributed to that factor.

questions.text: Event A: heavy rain fell throughout the night. Event B: the low-lying road was under water in the morning. Which relation is most reasonable?
options: B is the cause and A is the effect
Both are effects of an unrelated cause
There is no connection between them
A is the cause and B is the effect
questions.explanation: The rain preceded the flooding and is sufficient to explain water collecting on low ground.

questions.text: Which of the following is a necessary condition for ordinary combustion?
questions.explanation: Ordinary burning cannot occur without an oxidising agent, whereas the particular fuel or the weather may vary.

questions.text: 'Since the new mayor took office, road accidents have fallen.' Before crediting the mayor, one must first rule out
options: the geographical size of the city
the cost of building the roads
other changes such as new traffic rules or fewer vehicles on the road
questions.explanation: A causal claim survives only when alternative explanations for the same change have been eliminated.

questions.text: Question: should smoking be prohibited in enclosed public places? Which is the strongest argument?
options: No, because some people enjoy it
Yes, because the smoke inhaled by others damages their health
No, because smokers also pay taxes
questions.explanation: An argument is strong when it is relevant and rests on a substantial consequence, here harm to non-smokers.

questions.text: Question: should public transport fares be subsidised? Which of the following arguments is weak?
options: No, because the transport minister is personally unpopular
Yes, because low fares help low-income commuters
No, because subsidies enlarge the fiscal deficit
Yes, because cheaper transport reduces the use of private cars
questions.explanation: An argument that turns on a person rather than on the policy is irrelevant and therefore weak.

questions.text: A strong argument is one that is
options: held by a large number of people
relevant to the issue and supported by evidence
questions.explanation: Strength depends on relevance and evidential support, not on length, popularity or the speaker's fame.

questions.text: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument that wearing seat belts should be compulsory?
options: Seat belts are made of strong woven fabric
Most new cars are fitted with seat belts
Several other countries have such a law
Seat belts sharply reduce deaths in road accidents
questions.explanation: Direct evidence that the measure saves lives supports the case, while the other statements are merely incidental.

questions.text: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the claim that a town's new filtration plant has made its water safe?
options: The plant was inaugurated by a senior official
A few residents continue to buy bottled water
Tests taken after installation still show bacteria above the permitted limit
The plant cost more than was estimated
questions.explanation: Test results bearing directly on water quality contradict the claim; cost, ceremony and habit do not.

questions.text: An argument that offers only emotional appeal and no supporting evidence is best described as
questions.explanation: Without relevant evidence an argument fails to support its conclusion, however moving it may be.

questions.text: In evaluating arguments, 'relevance' means that the argument
options: is short and easy to read
bears directly on the question under discussion
questions.explanation: A relevant argument addresses the actual issue; irrelevant material cannot support the conclusion however true it is.

questions.text: Statement: cracks have appeared in a bridge carrying heavy traffic on a national highway. Which course of action is most appropriate?
options: Wait until the cracks widen further
Ban all vehicles throughout the province
Close the bridge to traffic and have it inspected at once
Raise the toll charged on the bridge
questions.explanation: The immediate danger to life requires the traffic to be stopped and the structure examined; the other steps are irrelevant or excessive.

questions.text: Statement: an outbreak of dengue fever has been reported in a city. Which course of action is most appropriate?
options: Close all schools in the country permanently
Prohibit the sale of mosquito nets
Shift the population of the city elsewhere
Remove stagnant water and spray the affected localities
questions.explanation: Dengue spreads through mosquitoes that breed in standing water, so removing breeding sites attacks the cause.

questions.text: Statement: an unusually large number of candidates failed a departmental examination this year. Which course of action is most appropriate?
options: Examine the reasons for the poor result and arrange remedial training
questions.explanation: Finding the cause before acting is the reasonable step; the other options either avoid the problem or punish without evidence.

questions.text: Statement: a public office receives repeated complaints about long queues at its counters. Which course of action is most appropriate?
options: Reduce the working hours of the office
Close half of the existing counters
Introduce an appointment and token system and open more counters at peak hours
questions.explanation: Managing the flow of visitors addresses the cause of the queues, while the other measures would worsen the situation.

questions.text: Statement: a school reports that many pupils arrive without breakfast and lose attention in class. Which course of action is most appropriate?
options: Start a school meal scheme and inform parents of the problem
Expel the pupils who lose attention
questions.explanation: Providing food and involving parents removes the stated cause of inattention; the other steps punish the pupils instead.
